name: Upper/lower split

lead: An upper/lower split divides weight training into upper-body days and lower-body days, usually run four days per week. Each muscle group is trained twice a week, with rest days between sessions.

People use it to build muscle size and strength, which shapes physique, shoulder width and overall build. Training frequency, intensity and volume are described in general references as the variables that drive muscle growth, and this layout is one way to organise them.

paras: A typical week alternates upper and lower sessions with rest days. Lifters on T Nation forums describe it as one of several common splits alongside the bro split and push/pull/legs, and one poster describes running a Wendler 'BBB Opposite' program as essentially an upper-lower split. Results over months depend on progressive overload, food and sleep.

Risks are those of weight training generally: strain and overuse injury if volume or load outstrips recovery. A four-day layout fits many schedules but offers fewer sessions per week than higher-frequency splits.

More muscle and a fuller physique over time
angle.text: The split is a way to schedule training so that each muscle group gets work twice a week. People use it to build shoulders, back, arms and legs for a more muscular physique.

lead: An upper/lower split is a weight-training layout that alternates sessions for the upper body and the lower body, most often across four training days a week. Pressing, pulling and arm work sit on upper days; squats, hinges and leg work sit on lower days. Because each half of the body is trained twice a week, it is one of the standard ways lifters organise muscle-building work, and it is discussed on T Nation alongside the bro split and the push/pull/legs split [1].

People use it to add muscle and strength, and through them to change physique: wider-looking shoulders, a fuller back and arms, and stronger legs. A general reference on muscle hypertrophy names training frequency, intensity and total volume as variables that affect growth, and says gradually increasing them produces hypertrophy [2]. A 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis of training frequency reported that, with volume equated, training a muscle twice a week produced superior hypertrophic outcomes to once a week, and that evidence for three sessions over two remains open [3]. Wikipedia's weight-training article summarises the same pattern [4]. A four-day upper/lower week meets the twice-weekly mark with two rest days.

Lifters on forums describe adapting other programs into this shape; one T Nation poster says that doing a Wendler 'BBB Opposite' program is essentially an upper-lower split, run with modifications [5]. Published research has compared splits as a category more than the upper/lower layout by name, so most claims about it are drawn from studies of frequency and volume.
infobox: About twice weekly per muscle group

paras: The layout divides the body into two halves. Upper sessions cover chest, back, shoulders and arms; lower sessions cover quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes and calves, with core work placed on either. A typical week runs upper, lower, rest, upper, lower, with the remaining days off, though lifters rearrange the order around their schedules. T Nation forum posts name it as a common choice beside the bro split and push/pull/legs [1].

Wikipedia describes a split as the way training volume is spread across the week, and lists full-body, upper/lower, push/pull/legs and the bro split as popular options [4]. In that taxonomy the upper/lower split sits between the full-body approach, which trains every muscle at each session, and body-part splits, which give each muscle a single dedicated day.

Dividing training by body region is long established in physique culture. Bodybuilding grew out of the late-19th-century displays of Eugen Sandow, and the IFBB, founded in 1946 by Joe and Ben Weider, helped build the magazine and contest culture in which routine design became a staple topic [6]. Wikipedia notes that weight training became far more popular after the 1977 film Pumping Iron and Arnold Schwarzenegger's rise [4]. The upper/lower split has no single inventor or founding date in the sources consulted; it is treated as a generic scheduling pattern rather than a named program.

In online lifting communities it is typically presented as a middle option: more frequent than a classic bro split, less frequent per muscle than a full-body routine, and fitting a four-day week. Training logs on T Nation show lifters mixing it with other methods, for example strength templates and body-part blocks [1][5].

The general hypertrophy reference lists frequency, intensity and total volume as variables that directly affect growth, and gives mechanical tension from progressive overload, acting through mTOR signalling and muscle protein synthesis, as the leading explanation [2]. It also says long-term gains appear to depend more on total volume and progressive overload than on repetition tempo [2].

Splitting weekly volume across two sessions per muscle is the layout's main rationale. Proponents say it gives each muscle group two stimuli a week without the long sessions that a once-a-week body-part day requires, and that having the upper and lower halves alternate lets each rest while the other works. The same reference describes nutrition and recovery as supporting factors: a positive energy balance over time, and protein intakes up to about 1.6 g/kg a day associated with gains in strength and size [2].

sections.h: How it is used to improve physique
paras: Lifters running an upper/lower week commonly place heavy compound lifts first in each session and add accessory work for shoulders, upper back and arms on upper days, which are the muscles that most influence how broad the frame looks. Lower days build the legs and glutes. Over months, progressive overload, adequate food and sleep, and consistency determine the result, as described in the hypertrophy literature [2].

Some forum users report using the split when they have limited time, when recovering from heavier training blocks, or when moving off a once-a-week body-part routine [1][5]. One T Nation discussion thread, in which posters argue that strength is relevant to physique improvement because 'form follows function', illustrates how lifters link heavier loading to appearance goals [7].

Variants include a four-day upper/lower with one strength-focused and one hypertrophy-focused session per half, and five- or six-day hybrids that add a third upper or lower day. Wikipedia notes that some programs alternate different splits week to week [4]. Competing layouts are the full-body routine, push/pull/legs and the bro split, which T Nation posters mention as the usual comparison set [1].

No studies found on the upper/lower split as a named program. Related research on training frequency exists: a 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis in Sports Medicine reported that, when volume was equated, training each muscle twice weekly gave better hypertrophy than once weekly [3]. Wikipedia's weight-training article states that for muscle growth two sessions per muscle per week outperform one, that whether three beats two is unresolved, and that when total volume is equal, frequency has no influence on strength gains [4]. A randomized trial in women who were not resistance trained compared split-body and full-body programs [8].

Wikipedia lists poor form as a source of strains and fractures and inadequate recovery as a source of fatigue and injury risk in weight training generally [4]. Bodybuilding references describe overtraining as workload exceeding recovery capacity, often alongside poor nutrition or sleep [6]. A four-day layout leaves rest days between sessions; lifters adjust volume and load around how they recover.

lore.intro: On T Nation and similar forums the upper/lower split is discussed as one of several standard weekly layouts, often adapted from other programs and compared with the bro split and push/pull/legs [1][5].

claims.claim: Training each muscle twice a week builds more muscle than once a week
A four-day upper/lower week is an efficient fit for a busy schedule
Many programs are 'essentially' an upper-lower split
Strength training with heavier loads is relevant to physique improvement
A bro split, with one dedicated day per muscle, suits some lifters better than higher-frequency splits
